lesson.title: Slash Notation: Squeezing a Subnet Mask into Two Characters
lesson.summary: CIDR notation writes a subnet mask as a slash followed by the count of leading 1 bits, replacing four dotted-decimal numbers with one small integer that is far easier to read and route on.
lesson.body:
Once you know that an IP address has a fixed 32-bit structure arranged as four octets, and that a subnet mask marks off the network portion with a run of leading 1 bits, CIDR notation, short for Classless Inter-Domain Routing, is almost trivial: instead of writing the mask out in full dotted-decimal form, you write the IP address followed by a slash and the number of 1 bits in the mask. The address 192.168.1.0 with mask 255.255.255.192 becomes 192.168.1.0/26. The slash number and the mask are two representations of the identical fact, and any network engineer needs to be able to convert fluently between them.

The conversion itself is simple bit counting. 255.255.255.0 has 24 leading 1 bits, eight full 1s in each of the first three octets, so it is /24. 255.255.255.128 has 25 leading 1 bits, so it is /25. 255.255.255.192 has 26, as shown in the subnet mask example, so it is /26. 255.255.255.224 has 27, so /27. Each additional 1 bit borrowed from the host portion cuts the number of addresses in the block in half: a /24 holds 256 addresses, a /25 holds 128, a /26 holds 64, and a /27 holds 32. Because the pattern is a clean count of bits rather than a fixed class boundary, CIDR notation can express any prefix length from /0, the entire address space, to /32, a single host, which is precisely what classless means: the old rigid Class A, B, and C boundaries at /8, /16, and /24 are gone, replaced by a mask that can end at any bit position.

CIDR was introduced in the 1990s specifically to slow the exhaustion of the IPv4 address space and to control the explosive growth of routing tables on the internet backbone. Before CIDR, an organization that needed 500 addresses had no efficient classful option: a Class C block only offered 254 usable host addresses, so it would have to be issued a full Class B block of over 65,000 addresses, wasting the rest. With CIDR, that same organization can be issued a /23, which combines two /24-sized blocks into 512 addresses, a far tighter fit. This efficiency also lets internet service providers aggregate many small customer blocks into one larger advertised route, a technique called route summarization, the direct ancestor of what this unit covers next as supernetting.

As a worked example, consider the block 10.4.16.0/22. A /22 means 22 network bits and 10 host bits, since 32 minus 22 equals 10. Ten host bits yield 2 to the 10th power, or 1024, total addresses, running from 10.4.16.0 through 10.4.19.255. Written as a dotted-decimal mask, that /22 is 255.255.252.0, because the third octet's binary value 11111100 contributes 6 more 1 bits on top of the 16 from the first two full octets.

Being able to move fluently between the slash number, the dotted mask, and the resulting address count is the core skill CIDR notation demands, and it is the same skill that subnetting and supernetting both build on directly in the sections that follow.
